"## History and founding of Wikipedia: Nupedia, Jimmy Wales, Larry Sanger, January 2001 launch, and major milestones
# History and Founding of Wikipedia — Research Summary

## Background: Bomis and Nupedia (2000)
- Jimmy Wales, co-owner of the web portal company **Bomis** (founded 1996 with Tim Shell), funded a free online encyclopedia project, **Nupedia**, launched **March 9, 2000** [1][2][5].
- **Larry Sanger**, a philosophy PhD and Bomis employee, was hired as Nupedia's editor-in-chief. Nupedia used a rigorous, expert-driven **seven-step review process**, which proved extremely slow: only about a dozen articles were approved in its first year, and fewer than 25 in its lifetime [1][2][10].
- In late 2000, programmer **Ben Kovitz** introduced Sanger to the wiki concept (Ward Cunningham's WikiWikiWeb) in a conversation in San Diego. Sanger proposed using a wiki to accelerate content creation, and Wales agreed [1][5][10].

## Launch of Wikipedia (January 2001)
- A wiki was attached to Nupedia on **January 10, 2001**; after Nupedia's editors balked, it was moved to its own site, **Wikipedia.com**, launching officially on **January 15, 2001** [1][2][5].
- Sanger **coined the name "Wikipedia"** (wiki + encyclopedia) and drafted the project's early policies, including the **"neutral point of view"** principle [3][10].
- The project was initially framed as a "feeder" for Nupedia, but grew far faster and quickly eclipsed it; Nupedia was shut down in **September 2003** [1][2].
- Richard Stallman's rival **GNUPedia** project, announced the same month, lent urgency and legitimacy to the free-encyclopedia idea before fading [1][5].

## Wales and Sanger: roles and the co-founder question
- **Wales** provided funding, infrastructure, and business oversight via Bomis; **Sanger** was the paid editorial leader and chief organizer during Wikipedia's first year [1][3][10].
- Sanger resigned on **March 1, 2002** after Bomis, hit by the dot-com downturn, ended his funding; he cited lack of respect from the community and discomfort with its anti-elitist culture [1][3].
- Early statements by Wales credited Sanger as co-founder, but from the mid-2000s Wales increasingly described himself as the sole founder; Wikipedia's own articles and most reference works treat **both men as co-founders**, while noting the dispute [1][3][9]. Sanger later founded Citizendium (2007) and became a prominent critic of Wikipedia's neutrality [3].

## Early growth (2001–2003)
- **1,000 English articles by February 12, 2001**; **10,000 by September 2001**; roughly 20,000 articles in 18 languages by the end of 2001 [1][5].
- First non-English editions (Catalan, German) appeared in **March 2001** [1].
- In February 2002, concerns about possible advertising triggered the Spanish-language fork **Enciclopedia Libre** [1].
- Custom software replaced UseModWiki: **Magnus Manske's PHP "Phase II"** (January 2002), then "Phase III," renamed **MediaWiki** in 2003 [1][5].

## Institutionalization and major milestones
- **June 20, 2003**: the nonprofit **Wikimedia Foundation** was established; Wikipedia adopted its iconic puzzle-globe logo the same year [1][8].
- **2004**: Webby Award and Prix Ars Electronica Golden Nica [1].
- **December 2005**: *Nature* found Wikipedia's science articles roughly comparable in accuracy to Encyclopædia Britannica's [7].
- **June 2009**: relicensed from GFDL to **Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike (CC BY-SA)** [1][8].
- **January 18, 2012**: 24-hour blackout in protest of SOPA/PIPA [1][12].
- **2012–2019**: Wikipedia Zero program provided free mobile access in developing countries [8].
- **January 15, 2021**: 20th anniversary; **January 15, 2026**: 25th anniversary [8][11].
- English Wikipedia article milestones: 100,000 (Jan 2003), 500,000 (Mar 2005), **1 million (Mar 1, 2006 — Jordanhill railway station)**, 2 million (Sept 2007), 3 million (Aug 2009), 4 million (Apr 2013), 5 million (Nov 2015), 6 million (Jan 2020), and **7 million in late 2025** [1][8].
- As of 2026, Wikipedia spans **300+ language editions with roughly 65 million total articles**, is consistently among the world's ten most-visited websites, and is funded by donations to the Wikimedia Foundation rather than advertising [8][9][12].

## Scale and statistics of Wikipedia: number of articles, language editions, active editors, and edit counts (latest available figures)
# Wikipedia: Scale & Statistics

*Note: I cannot run live queries in this session, so figures below are the latest I can verify (as of early–mid 2025), with clearly-flagged estimates for 2026. Live counters: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Statistics and stats.wikimedia.org.*

## 1. Articles
- **All language editions combined:** ~**64 million** articles (early 2025) [1][2]; growing ~2–3M/year, so ~66M estimated by late 2026.
- **English Wikipedia:** ~**6.9 million** articles (early 2025) [3]. Milestones: 6 millionth article on 23 Jan 2020 [5]; at ~15k new articles/month, it likely crossed **7 million in late 2025/early 2026** (~7.1–7.2M estimated for Sep 2026) [3].
- **Largest editions** (approx., early 2025, millions of articles) [1][2]:

| Edition | Articles | | Edition | Articles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| English | 6.9 | | Russian | 2.0 |
| Cebuano | 6.1 | | Spanish | 2.0 |
| German | 2.9 | | Italian | 1.9 |
| French | 2.65 | | Polish | 1.6 |
| Swedish | 2.5 | | Japanese | ~1.45 |
| Dutch | 2.1 | | Chinese | ~1.45 |

- Caveat: Cebuano and Swedish totals are largely bot-created (Lsjbot stubs) [2].

## 2. Language editions
- **342 total editions; 329 active** (early 2024, latest verified) — a handful added since, so ~330 active in 2025 [2]. Several dozen closed/inactive editions (e.g., Muscogee, Choctaw) exist [2].

## 3. Editors
- **Monthly active editors** (≥5 edits in 30 days):
  - English Wikipedia: ~**42,000–44,000** [1][3]
  - All Wikipedia editions: ~**200,000**
  - All Wikimedia projects (incl. Commons, Wikidata): ~**250,000–265,000** [1][4]
- Very active editors (≥100 edits/month): ~10,000–11,000 on English Wikipedia [1][3].
- English Wikipedia registered accounts: ~**47 million** (mostly dormant) [3].
- Trend: active-editor counts have been roughly flat/slightly declining since a mid-2000s peak [1][4].

## 4. Edits
- **English Wikipedia lifetime edits:** surpassed **1 billion on 13 Jan 2021** [5]; ~**1.3 billion** by 2025 [3]. Current rate: ~**5.5–6 million edits/month** (~2/second), including bot edits [1][3].
- **All editions combined:** roughly **15 million edits/month** on Wikipedias; ~**20+ million/month** across all Wikimedia projects (~7–8 edits/second) — approximate, per Wikistats [1].
- Bots account for a substantial share of edits (varies widely by wiki; extreme on bot-built editions) [1][2].
- English Wikipedia also holds ~61 million total pages (incl. talk/user pages) and ~900k files [3].

## Governance and content policies: neutral point of view, verifiability, no original research, editors/administrators, Arbitration Committee, Wikimedia Foundation
## Findings

**Wikipedia’s governance model is community-driven.** The Wikimedia Foundation hosts and operates the platform, but article content and most local policies are developed and enforced by volunteer editors through consensus. [1][7][8]

### Core content policies
Wikipedia’s three core content policies are:

1. **Neutral point of view (NPOV)** — Articles must represent significant published views fairly, proportionately, and without editorial bias; minority and majority views are weighted according to their prominence in reliable sources. [2]
2. **Verifiability** — Article material must be attributable to reliable published sources; challenged or likely-to-be-challenged claims need inline citations. Verifiability is the inclusion threshold, even if editors believe a claim is true. [3]
3. **No original research (NOR)** — Wikipedia does not publish unpublished facts, arguments, data, or novel analysis. Content must come from published reliable sources; synthesis that advances a claim not made by the sources is not allowed. [4]

### Editors and administrators
- **Editors** are volunteers who write, revise, source, and discuss content. Policy is normally shaped through community consensus, not by a central editorial board. [5][7]
- **Administrators** are experienced editors with extra technical tools—such as page protection, deletion, and blocking—to enforce community decisions and prevent disruption. They do not “own” articles and do not have extra authority over content merely because they are admins. [6]

### Arbitration Committee
The **Arbitration Committee (ArbCom)** is Wikipedia’s highest internal dispute-resolution body for serious user-conduct disputes. It can issue binding remedies such as editing restrictions, topic bans, site bans, and removal of administrator permissions. It generally addresses conduct rather than directly deciding article text. [7]

### Wikimedia Foundation
The **Wikimedia Foundation** is the nonprofit organization that operates Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. It provides infrastructure, legal support, trademarks, funding, and global platform governance, but it normally does not set article content or decide day-to-day editorial disputes. [8]

## Reliability, accuracy studies, vandalism, and major criticisms including systemic bias and gender gap
# Wikipedia: Reliability, Vandalism, and Criticisms — Research Summary

## Accuracy & Reliability Studies

- **Nature 2005 comparison**: In the most cited study, Nature had experts review 42 science articles from Wikipedia and Encyclopædia Britannica blind. Wikipedia averaged 3.86 inaccuracies per article vs. Britannica's 2.92 (162 vs. 123 total), with 4 "serious errors" in each [1]. Britannica published a rebuttal calling the study "fatally flawed"; Nature stood by its findings [2].
- **Expert readership**: Chesney (2006) found experts rated Wikipedia articles *more* accurate than non-experts did, and more accurate than they expected [3].
- **Medical content**: Hasty et al. (2014, *JAOA*) found 9 of 10 Wikipedia articles on the 10 costliest US medical conditions contained claims contradicted by peer-reviewed literature [4]. Kräenbring et al. (2014, *JMIR*) found most of 100 Wikipedia drug articles accurate but **incomplete** relative to standard pharmacology textbooks, with completeness tracking article quality ratings [5].
- **Overall scholarly consensus**: quality is broadly comparable to traditional encyclopedias for general topics, variable in specialized fields, and improving over time.

## Vandalism

- **Speed of repair**: Viégas, Wattenberg & McKeon (2007) found most blatant vandalism is reverted within minutes — median repair time under ~3 minutes on heavily watched pages [10]. Machine-learning tools (ClueBot NG, ORES) and semi-protection now handle most cases.
- **Seigenthaler incident (2005)**: A false biography linking John Seigenthaler Sr. to the JFK assassination persisted 132 days, prompting tightening of the "Biographies of Living Persons" policy and requiring accounts to create articles [11].
- **Essjay controversy (2007)**: A top editor's fabricated academic credentials (exposed via a New Yorker correction) triggered credential-verification debates [12].
- **Wikipedia Scanner (2007)**: IP tracing exposed edits from US congressional staff, the CIA/FBI, and corporate whitewashing (e.g., Diebold, ExxonMobil) [13].
- **Long-lived hoaxes**: "Jar'Edo Wens," a fake Aboriginal deity, survived ~10 years (2003–2014) [14]; the fabricated "Bicholim Conflict" lasted five years before deletion (2012) [15].
- **Paid editing**: The 2015 "Orangemoody" investigation blocked ~280 accounts running undisclosed paid-editing/extortion schemes [23].

## Systemic Bias

- **Definition**: Wikipedia acknowledges bias arising from its skewed editor base (predominantly male, Western, technically inclined).
- **Geographic**: Oxford Internet Institute "Mapping Wikipedia" work found geotagged coverage heavily concentrated in Europe and North America, with Africa and parts of Asia severely underrepresented [9].
- **Ideological**: Greenstein & Zhu (2018, *MIS Quarterly*) found Wikipedia articles were historically slanted Democratic/left relative to Britannica, but bias moderated as the editor base diversified [6]. A 2024 Manhattan Institute analysis by David Rozado reported asymmetric negative framing of right-leaning figures and topics [7]. Co-founder Larry Sanger (2021) publicly claimed the site has become "badly biased," especially on political topics [8]. The 2018 "Philip Cross affair" — a single editor making tens of thousands of edits to political commentators' pages — fueled accountability criticisms [24].
- **Structural**: Reliance on mainstream media for notability and sourcing disadvantages under-covered regions, cultures, and historical actors, feeding deletionism disputes.

## Gender Gap

- **Editors**: A 2011 Wikimedia Foundation survey found only ~9% of editors were women [16]. Sue Gardner's "Nine Reasons Why Women Don't Edit Wikipedia" (2011) framed the problem publicly [16]. Lam et al.'s "WP:Clubhouse" (2011) found women concentrated in less-visible roles and deterred by social dynamics [17]. A 2018 MIT cross-language study (PLOS ONE) found women remain a minority of editors in every language edition studied [19].
- **Content**: Women's biographies rose from ~15% (2014) to roughly 19–20% (2024–25) of English Wikipedia biographies, per Wikidata/Humaniki tracking [20]. Wagner et al. (2015, "It's a Man's Wikipedia?") found women's biographies more likely to be missing, articles about women linking disproportionately to men, and notability criteria disadvantaging women [18]. Adams & Brückner (2015; 2021) found biographies of women draw on fewer sources and cite disproportionately fewer works by women scholars [22].
- **Notable flashpoint**: The 2013 "American women novelists" subcategory controversy (Amanda Filipacchi's NYT op-ed) crystallized criticism of male-default framing [21].
- **Remediation**: Women in Red (2015–), Art+Feminism edit-a-thons (2014–), and WikiProject Women Scientists target both editor and content gaps.

## Other Recurring Criticisms

- Edit wars, deletionism, and administrator accountability gaps; circular reporting with news media; undisclosed conflict-of-interest editing (e.g., the Bell Pottinger exposé, 2011) [25].

## Cultural impact of Wikipedia: web traffic rankings, role as AI training data source, recognition and awards
**Note:** No live search results were available in this session, so I cannot assign [N] index numbers. Findings below draw on well-established reporting; sources are named inline. Figures reflect my training data and may have changed since.

## Web Traffic
- Wikipedia.org is consistently ranked among the **top 10 most-visited websites globally** (Similarweb; previously Alexa until its 2022 retirement), typically #5–10 alongside Google, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, X, WhatsApp, and Reddit.
- Wikimedia Foundation stats show roughly **1.5+ billion unique devices per month**; English Wikipedia alone draws ~10 billion pageviews monthly, with all language editions combined substantially higher.
- Guinness World Records recognizes it as the **largest encyclopedia ever compiled**; it is widely described as the largest and most-read reference work in history (~7 million English articles; ~60+ million across all languages as of the mid-2020s).

## Role as AI Training Data
- Wikipedia is a **core corpus in virtually every major LLM**, including OpenAI's GPT series, Google's BERT/T5, and Meta's LLaMA, via datasets like The Pile, C4 (Common Crawl), RedPajama, and Dolma — valued for quality, structure, and permissive CC BY-SA licensing.
- It underpins foundational NLP artifacts: the SQuAD question-answering benchmark, DBpedia/Wikidata knowledge graphs, and entity-linking systems; it grounds Google's Knowledge Graph and major voice assistants.
- **Wikimedia Enterprise** (launched 2021) sells structured bulk access; 2024 Wired reporting revealed Google, Meta, and Amazon among paying customers, driven largely by AI demand.
- In 2025, Wikimedia reported **human pageviews declined ~8% year-over-year**, attributed partly to AI chatbots and search summaries answering questions without sending traffic — prompting the Foundation to ask AI companies to attribute content and link back.
- The community is actively contending with a flood of AI-generated low-quality submissions, tightening policies accordingly.

## Recognition and Awards
- **2015 Erasmus Prize** awarded to the Wikipedia community (theme: digital culture), shared with the Internet Archive.
- **2015 Princess of Asturias Award** for International Cooperation (Spain).
- **Webby Award** for Community (2004).
- Unusual honors: **Wikipedia Monument** in Słubice, Poland (2014, first monument to the site) and asteroid **274301 Wikipedia** named by the IAU (2013).
- Cultural standing: commentators (e.g., Charlie Warzel in *The Atlantic*, 2023) have called it "the last best place on the internet," and it is frequently cited as a last line of defense for shared factual consensus in the AI-misinformation era."
